{{Short description|Unit of measure for digital data}}
{{Redirect-distinguish|tribit|Tebibit{{!}}tibit|Ternary numeral system{{!}}trit}}

A '''unit of information''' is any [[Unit of measurement|unit of measure]] of [[digital data]] size. In digital [[computing]], a unit of information is used to describe the capacity of a digital [[digital data storage|data storage]] device. In [[telecommunication]]s, a unit of information is used to describe the [[Network throughput|throughput]] of a [[communication channel]]. In [[information theory]], a unit of information is used to measure [[information]] contained in messages and the [[Entropy (information theory)|entropy]] of random variables.

Due to the need to work with data sizes that range from small to large, units of information cover a wide range of data sizes. Units are defined as multiples of a smaller unit except for the smallest unit which is based on convention and hardware design. [[Unit prefix|Multiplier prefixes]] are used to describe relatively large sizes.

For [[binary number|binary]] [[computer hardware|hardware]], the most common hardware today, the smallest unit is the [[bit]], which represents a value that is one of two possibilities, typically shown as 0 and 1. The [[nibble]], 4 bits, represents the value of a single [[hexadecimal]] digit. The [[byte]] (8 bits, 2 nibbles) is possibly the most commonly known and used base unit to describe data size. The [[Word (computer architecture)|word]] is a size that varies by and has a special importance for a particular hardware context. On modern hardware, a word is typically 2, 4 or 8 bytes, but the size varies dramatically on older hardware. Larger sizes can be expressed as multiples of a base unit via [[International System of Units|SI]] [[metric prefix]]es (powers of ten) or the newer and generally more accurate [[International Electrotechnical Commission|IEC]] [[binary prefix]]es (powers of two).

== Information theory ==
[[File:Units of information.svg|thumb|right|384px|Comparison of units of information: [[bit]], [[ternary numeral system|trit]], [[nat (unit)|nat]], [[ban (unit)|ban]]. Quantity of information is the height of bars. Dark green level is the "nat" unit.]]
{{Fundamental info units}}
In 1928, [[Ralph Hartley]] observed a fundamental storage principle,<ref name="Abramson_1963"/> which was further formalized by [[Claude Shannon]] in 1945: the information that can be stored in a system is proportional to the [[logarithm]] of ''N'' possible states of that system, denoted {{nowrap|log<sub>''b''</sub> ''N''}}. Changing the base of the logarithm from ''b'' to a different number ''c'' has the effect of multiplying the value of the logarithm by a fixed constant, namely {{nowrap|1=log<sub>''c''</sub> ''N'' = (log<sub>''c''</sub> ''b'') log<sub>''b''</sub> ''N''}}.
Therefore, the choice of the base ''b'' determines the unit used to measure information. In particular, if ''b'' is a [[positive and negative numbers|positive]] integer, then the unit is the amount of information that can be stored in a system with ''b'' possible states.

When ''b'' is 2, the unit is the [[Shannon (unit)|shannon]], equal to the [[information content]] of one "bit". A system with 8 possible states, for example, can store up to {{nowrap|1=log<sub>2</sub> 8 = 3}} bits of information. Other units that have been named include:
; Base ''b''&nbsp;=&nbsp;3 : the unit is called "[[ternary numeral system|trit]]", and is equal to {{nowrap|log<sub>2</sub> 3}} (≈&nbsp;1.585) bits.<ref name="Knuth"/>
; Base ''b''&nbsp;=&nbsp;10 : the unit is called ''[[decimal]] [[numerical digit|digit]]'', ''[[Hartley (unit)|hartley]]'', ''ban'', ''decit'', or ''dit'', and is equal to log<sub>2</sub>&nbsp;10 (≈ 3.322) bits.<ref name="Abramson_1963"/><ref name="Shanmugam_2006"/><ref name="Jaeger_2007"/><ref name="Kumar_2001"/>
; Base ''b''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''e'', the [[base of natural logarithm]]s : the unit is called a ''[[nat (unit)|nat]]'', ''nit'', or ''nepit'' (from [[John Napier|Neperian]]), and is worth {{nowrap|log<sub>2</sub> ''e''}} (≈&nbsp;1.443) bits.<ref name="Abramson_1963"/>
The trit, ban, and nat are rarely used to measure storage capacity. But the nat, in particular, is often used in information theory, because natural logarithms are mathematically more convenient than logarithms in other bases.

== Units derived from bit ==
Several conventional names are used for collections or groups of bits.

=== Byte ===
Historically, a [[byte]] was the number of bits used to encode a [[character (computing)|character]] of text in the computer, which depended on computer hardware architecture, but today it almost always means eight bits – that is, an [[octet (computing)|octet]]. An 8-bit byte can represent 256 distinct values, such as non-negative integers from 0 to 255, or [[two's complement|signed]] integers from −128 to 127. The [[IEEE&nbsp;1541-2002]] standard specifies "B" (upper case) as the symbol for byte ([[IEC&nbsp;80000-13]] uses "o" for octet in French, but also allows "B" in English). Bytes, or multiples thereof, are almost always used to specify the sizes of computer files and the capacity of storage units. Most modern computers and peripheral devices are designed to manipulate data in whole bytes or groups of bytes, rather than individual bits.

=== Nibble ===
A group of four bits, or half a byte, is sometimes called a [[nibble]], nybble or nyble. This unit is most often used in the context of [[hexadecimal]] number representations, since a nibble has the same number of possible values as one hexadecimal digit has.<ref name="Nybble"/>

=== Word, block, and page ===
Computers usually manipulate bits in groups of a fixed size, conventionally called ''[[word (computer architecture)|word]]s''. The number of bits in a word is usually defined by the size of the [[register (computing)|register]]s in the computer's [[CPU]], or by the number of data bits that are fetched from its [[main memory]] in a single operation. In the [[IA-32]] architecture more commonly known as x86-32, a word is 32 bits, but other past and current architectures use words with 4, 8, 9, 12, 13, 16, 18, 20, 21, 22, 24, 25, <!-- 26, not in Beebe! --> 29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 35, 36, 38, 39, 40, 42, 44, 48, 50, 52, 54, 56, 60, 64, 72<ref name="Beebe_2017"/> <!-- 80, not in Beebe! --> bits or others.

Some [[machine instruction]]s and [[computer number format]]s use two words (a "double word" or "dword"), or four words (a "quad word" or "quad").

Computer [[memory cache]]s usually operate on ''[[block (data storage)|block]]s'' of memory that consist of several consecutive words. These units are customarily called ''cache blocks'', or, in [[CPU cache]]s, ''cache lines''.

[[Virtual memory]] systems partition the computer's [[main storage]] into even larger units, traditionally called ''[[page (computer memory)|page]]s''.

=== Multiplicative prefixes ===

A unit for a large amount of data can be formed using either a [[Metric prefix|metric]] or binary prefix with a base unit. For storage, the base unit is typically a byte. For communication throughput, a base unit of bit is common. For example, using the metric ''kilo'' prefix, a [[kilobyte]] is 1000 bytes and a [[kilobit]] is 1000 bits.

Use of metric prefixes is common. In the context of computing, some of these prefixes (primarily ''kilo'', ''mega'' and ''giga'') are used to refer to the nearest power of two. For example, 'kilobyte' often refers to 1024 bytes even though the standard meaning of kilo is 1000.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2010-01-13 |title=Metric (SI) Prefixes |url=https://www.nist.gov/pml/owm/metric-si-prefixes |website=[[NIST]] |language=en}}</ref>

The [[JEDEC memory standards|JEDEC memory standard]] JESD88F notes that its inclusion of the definitions of kilo (K), mega (M) and giga (G) based on powers of two are included only to reflect common usage, but that these are otherwise deprecated.<ref name="JEDEC_2018_Terms"/>

== Size examples ==
* 1&nbsp;bit: Answer to a yes/no question
* 1&nbsp;byte: A number from 0 to 255
* 90&nbsp;bytes: Enough to store a typical line of text from a book
* 512&nbsp;bytes&nbsp;= 0.5&nbsp;KiB: The typical [[disk sector|sector]] size of an old style [[hard disk drive]] (modern [[Advanced Format]] sectors are 4096 bytes).
* 1024&nbsp;bytes&nbsp;= 1&nbsp;KiB: A [[block (data storage)|block]] size in some older [[UNIX]] [[filesystem]]s
* 2048&nbsp;bytes&nbsp;= 2&nbsp;KiB: A [[CD-ROM]] sector
* 4096&nbsp;bytes&nbsp;= 4&nbsp;KiB: A [[memory page]] in [[x86]] (since [[Intel 80386]]) and many other architectures, also the modern [[Advanced Format]] hard disk drive sector size.
* 4&nbsp;kB: About one page of text from a [[novel]]
* 120&nbsp;kB: The text of a typical pocket book
* 1&nbsp;MiB: A 1024×1024 pixel [[bitmap]] image with 256 colors (8&nbsp;bpp color depth)
* 3&nbsp;MB: A three-minute [[song]] (133&nbsp;kbit/s)
* 650–900&nbsp;MB – a CD-ROM
* 1&nbsp;GB: 114 minutes of uncompressed CD-quality audio at 1.4&nbsp;Mbit/s
* 16&nbsp;GB: DDR5 DRAM laptop memory under $40 (as of early 2024)<!-- E.g. (and DDR4 or 3 even cheaper, down to $20): New Samsung 16GB (8GBX2) DDR5 4800 MHz PC5-38400 SODIMM Laptop Memory RAM (M425R1GB4BB0) OEM -->; about $169 (as of early 2026) due to the [[2025–present global memory supply shortage]]
* 32&nbsp;GB: SODIMM DDR5 DRAM laptop memory for $377.99 (as of early 2026)
* 32/64/128&nbsp;GB: Three common sizes of [[USB flash drive]]s
* 1&nbsp;TB: The size of a $30 hard disk (as of early 2024)
* 6&nbsp;TB: The size of a $100 hard disk (as of early 2022)
* 12&nbsp;TB game [[hard disk drive]] (for Xbox).
* 16&nbsp;TB: The size of a small/cheap $130 (as of early 2024) enterprise SAS hard disk drive
* 26&nbsp;TB: The size of $325 (as of early 2026) "video" hard disk drive <!-- 24TB here, more costly, was previously cheapest per TB, that large, I could find: Seagate Skyhawk AI 24TB Video Internal Hard Drive HDD -->
* 44&nbsp;TB: Largest [[hard disk drive]] (as of {{as of|2026|3|lc=y}}, still only sold to data centers; 36&nbsp;TB in Feb 2025 was then also only sold to data centers).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Shilov |first=Anton |date=2026-03-03 |title=Seagate begins shipping 44TB hard drives with HAMR tech to data centers — Mozaic 4+ platform expands to 10 platters |url=https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/hdds/seagate-begins-shipping-44tb-hard-drives-with-hamr-tech-to-data-centers-mozaic-4-platform-expands-to-10-platters |access-date=2026-04-17 |website=Tom's Hardware |language=en}}</ref>
* 100&nbsp;TB: Largest commercially available [[solid-state drive]] (as of mid-2024)
* 200&nbsp;TB: Largest solid-state drive constructed (prediction for mid-2022)<!-- Likely never materialized? -->
* 1.6&nbsp;PB (1600&nbsp;TB): Amount of possible storage in one 2U server (world record as of 2021, using 100&nbsp;TB solid-states drives).<!--"use ExaDrive SSDs, including the 100TB capable ExaDrive DC series and QLC-based ExaDrive NL series, in PowerEdge servers. [..] enabling up to 1.2PB of flash in one 2U server. [..]
[As of 2024] As the world’s highest capacity and highest density SSD, ExaDrive offers capacity, energy efficiency, and endurance, thanks to patent-pending architecture. It is available in capacities ranging from 16TB to 100TB, using either SATA or dual-port SAS interfaces, with both TLC and QLC flash models."--><ref>{{Cite web |last=Maleval |first=Jean Jacques |date=2021-02-12 |title=Nimbus Data SSDs Certified for Use With Dell EMC PowerEdge Servers |url=https://www.storagenewsletter.com/2021/02/12/nimbus-data-ssds-certified-by-dell-emc-for-poweredge-servers/ |access-date=2024-05-30 |website=StorageNewsletter |language=en-US}}</ref>

Some notable unit names that are today obsolete or only used in limited contexts. 

* 1 bit: unibit<ref name="Horak_2007_Websters"/><ref name="YourDict_Unibit"/>

* 2 bits: dibit,<ref name="Steinbuch-Wagner_1967"/><ref name="Steinbuch-Weber_1974"/><ref name="Horak_2007_Websters"/><ref name="Bertram_1994"/> crumb,<ref name="Weisstein_Crumb"/> quartic digit,<ref name="CDC_1964"/> quad, semi-nibble, nyp<ref name="Knuth_Nyp"/>

* 3 bits: tribit,<ref name="Steinbuch-Wagner_1967"/><ref name="Steinbuch-Weber_1974"/><ref name="Horak_2007_Websters"/> triad,<ref name="Svoboda_1979"/> triade<ref name="Paul_2013_EE"/><ref name="Böhme_1969"/>

* 4 bits: see [[nibble]]

* 5 bits: pentad, pentade,<ref name="Speiser_1965"/>

* 6 bits: byte (in early [[IBM]] machines using [[BCD alphameric]]s), hexad, hexade,<ref name="Speiser_1965"/><ref name="Steinbuch_1962"/> sextet<ref name="Svoboda_1979"/>

* 7 bits: heptad, heptade<ref name="Speiser_1965"/>

* 8 bits: [[octad (computing)|octad]],<ref name="Williams_1969">{{cite book |title=British Commercial Computer Digest: Pergamon Computer Data Series |author-first=R. H. |author-last=Williams |publisher=[[Pergamon Press]] |date=1969-01-01 |isbn=1-48312210-7 |id=978-148312210-6 }}</ref> [[octade (computing)|octade]]<ref name="Philips_1971">{{cite web |title=Philips – Philips Data Systems' product range – April 1971 |publisher=[[Philips]] |date=1971 |url=http://www.intact-reunies.nl/pdf/product1971.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150917144504/http://www.intact-reunies.nl/pdf/product1971.pdf |url-status=usurped |archive-date=17 September 2015 |access-date=2015-08-03}}</ref>

* 9 bits: nonet,<ref name="Crispin_2005"/> rarely used

* 10 bits: declet,<ref name="IEEE754-2008"/><ref name="Muller_2010"/><ref name="Erle_2008"/><ref name="Kneusel_2015"/> decle<ref name="Zbiciak"/>

* 12 bits: [[slab (unit)|slab]]<ref name="NCR_315_EDPS"/><ref name="Bardin_1963"/><ref name="Schneider_1970"/>

* 15 bits: parcel (on [[CDC 6600]] and [[CDC 7600]])

* 16 bits: doublet,<ref name="IEEE1754-1994"/> wyde,<ref name="Knuth"/><ref name="Knuth_MMIX"/> parcel (on [[Cray-1]]), chawmp (on a 32-bit machine)<ref name="Raymond_HackerDict">{{cite book |last1=Raymond |first1=Eric S. |title=The New Hacker's Dictionary |date=1996 |publisher=MIT Press |isbn=0262680920 |page=333 |edition=3}}</ref>

* 18 bits: chomp, chawmp (on a 36-bit machine)<ref name="Raymond_HackerDict"/>

* 32 bits: quadlet,<ref name="IEEE1754-1994"/><ref name="ParNum_1999"/><ref name="Nicoud_1999"/> tetra<ref name="Knuth_MMIX"/>

* 64 bits: octlet,<ref name="IEEE1754-1994"/> octa<ref name="Knuth_MMIX"/>

* 96 bits: bentobox (in [[ITRON project|ITRON OS]])

* 128 bits: hexlet,<ref name="IEEE1754-1994"/><ref name="SEDMS_1999"/> [[paragraph (Intel)|paragraph]] (on [[Intel x86]] processors)<ref name="Intel_1980_8086FU-UG"/><ref name="Dewar-Smosna_1990"/>

* 256 bytes: [[page (computer memory)|page]] (on Intel 4004,<ref name="Intel_1973_MCS-4"/> [[Intel 8080|8080]] and 8086 processors,<ref name="Intel_1980_8086FU-UG"/> also many other 8-bit processors&nbsp;– typically much larger on many 16-bit/32-bit processors)

* 6 trits: [[tryte]]<ref name="Brousentsov_Tryte"/>

* combit, comword<ref name="Telefunken_1979"/><ref name="US4319227_1"/><ref name="US4319227_2"/>
